n: Jesus finishes his final discourse. Matthew’s formula now says “all these sayings” — the teaching ministry is complete, and the story turns to his suffering.

f.w: when Jesus had finished all these sayings

n: Jesus knows exactly what is coming: Passover is two days away, and he will be handed over to be crucified. He goes forward willingly.

f.g: The annual festival remembering Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, when a lamb was sacrificed.

n: Meanwhile the leaders meet at the residence of Caiaphas, the high priest.

f.g: High priest from about AD 18 to 36, son-in-law of the former high priest Annas.

n: They plot to arrest Jesus by stealth and have him killed.

f.g: subtilty = cunning, deceit, trickery.

n: They want to avoid the festival itself, fearing a riot among the huge Passover crowds who admired Jesus.

f.g: Jerusalem’s population swelled dramatically at Passover.

n: In Bethany, Jesus dines at the home of Simon the leper — likely someone Jesus had healed.
A woman — John identifies her as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus — pours very costly perfumed oil on Jesus’s head.

f.g: A sealed flask of soft stone; it was broken to pour out the contents.
Anointing the head recalls how kings were anointed.

n: The disciples are indignant at what they see as waste.

f.w: To what purpose is this waste?
f.g: John says Judas led this complaint.

n: They reason the perfume could have been sold and the money given to the poor. Mark says it was worth over 300 denarii — about a year’s wages.
Jesus defends her: she has done a beautiful thing for him.

f.g: Done a beautiful, noble deed.

n: There will always be chances to help the poor, but only a little time left to honor him in person.

f.w: ye have the poor always with you

n: Her act anointed his body ahead of his burial. She seems to understand what the disciples don’t.

f.w: she did it for my burial

n: Jesus promises her act of devotion will be remembered wherever the gospel is preached — and it still is.

f.g: As a way of remembering her.

n: In sharp contrast to the woman’s generosity, Judas, one of the Twelve, goes to the chief priests.
Judas asks what they’ll pay to have Jesus handed over. They agree on thirty silver coins — the legal price of a slave.

f.g: Agreed, made a deal; or literally “weighed out.”

n: From then on Judas watches for a chance to betray Jesus quietly.
On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples ask where to prepare the Passover meal.

f.g: A seven-day festival joined to Passover, when no yeast was eaten.

n: Jesus sends them to a particular man in the city to arrange a room. He knows his “time” has arrived.

f.g: A certain person — left unnamed, perhaps to keep the location secret from Judas.

n: The disciples follow his directions and prepare the Passover.

f.g: Preparing the lamb, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, and wine.

n: At evening Jesus reclines at the table with the Twelve.

f.g: Reclined — Passover was eaten reclining, as free people.

n: During the meal Jesus makes a devastating announcement: one of them will betray him.

f.w: one of you shall betray me

n: Deeply grieved, each asks, “Lord, is it I?” — humbly examining himself instead of accusing others.

f.g: The Greek form expects the answer “no” — “Surely not I, Lord?”

n: The betrayer is someone sharing the common dish with him — a close companion. Sharing a meal implied loyalty and friendship.

f.w: He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish

n: Jesus’s death fulfills scripture, yet the betrayer is still fully responsible for his choice.

f.w: as it is written of him
if he had not been born

n: Judas asks the same question, calling Jesus “Rabbi” rather than “Lord.” Jesus’s answer, “You have said it,” quietly confirms it.

f.g: Greek rhabbi — a teacher’s title, unlike the others’ “Lord.”
An idiom meaning “Yes — your words, not mine.”

n: Jesus takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and gives it to them: “This is my body.” This institutes the sacrament.

f.g: The JST adds that the bread is “in remembrance of my body.”

n: He takes the cup, gives thanks, and tells them all to drink from it.

f.g: Greek eucharisteō.

n: The wine represents his blood, which seals a new covenant and is shed for the forgiveness of sins.

f.g: testament = covenant.
Forgiveness, release.

n: He won’t drink wine again until he drinks it new with them in his Father’s kingdom — a promise of future reunion.

f.w: until that day when I drink it new with you

n: They sing a hymn — traditionally the Hallel psalms closing the Passover — and go out to the Mount of Olives.

f.g: Probably part of Psalms 113–118, sung at Passover.

n: Jesus tells them they will all desert him that night, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of the stricken shepherd.

f.g: Stumble, fall away.

n: But he promises that after rising, he will go ahead of them to Galilee — hope even amid the warning.

f.w: I will go before you into Galilee

n: Peter insists that even if everyone else falls away, he never will.

f.w: yet will I never be offended

n: Jesus foretells that before the rooster crows that very night, Peter will deny him three times.

f.g: Before dawn; “cockcrow” also named the watch from about midnight to 3 a.m.
thrice = three times.

n: Peter vows he would die rather than deny Jesus, and all the disciples say the same. Their love is sincere, but they don’t yet know their own weakness.

f.w: Though I should die with thee

n: They reach Gethsemane, an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives. Jesus asks most of them to wait while he prays.

f.g: Aramaic for “oil press,” where olives were crushed for oil.

n: He takes Peter, James, and John further in, and begins to feel overwhelming sorrow and distress.

f.g: Deeply distressed, weighed down.

n: Jesus confides that his anguish is crushing him nearly to death, and asks them to stay awake with him.

f.w: My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death

n: Falling to the ground, he prays: if possible, let this cup pass — yet your will, not mine. Here Jesus begins to take on himself the sins and suffering of all.

f.w: let this cup pass from me
not as I will, but as thou wilt

n: Returning, he finds the disciples asleep and asks Peter, “Couldn’t you watch with me even one hour?”

f.w: could ye not watch with me one hour?

n: He urges them to watch and pray to resist temptation. Their spirit wants to do right, but the body is weak.

f.w: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak

n: He prays a second time, now accepting that he must drink the cup: “Thy will be done.”
Again he finds them asleep, unable to keep their eyes open.

f.g: Luke says they were sleeping for sorrow.

n: A third time he goes and prays the same prayer.
Returning, he tells them the hour has come; he is being handed over to sinners.

f.g: Possibly a question: “Are you still sleeping?”

n: “Get up, let’s go” — Jesus goes forward to meet his betrayer rather than fleeing.
Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests and elders.

f.g: staves = clubs, sticks.

n: Judas had arranged a signal: the one he kisses is Jesus. In the dark, they needed to be sure who to seize.

f.g: A kiss was a common greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

n: He goes straight up, greets Jesus, and kisses him — a sign of affection turned into betrayal.

f.g: A greeting, like “Greetings!”
The Greek implies an intense or prolonged kiss.

n: Jesus still calls Judas “friend” and asks him to do what he came for. Then they seize Jesus.

f.g: Greek hetairos — companion; also used in 20:13 and 22:12.
Possibly “Do what you came to do.”

n: One disciple — John names him as Peter — draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant.

f.g: John names the servant Malchus; Luke says Jesus healed the ear.

n: Jesus tells him to put the sword away. Violence only breeds more violence; his kingdom is not won that way.

f.w: all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword

n: If Jesus wanted rescue, his Father would instantly send more than twelve legions of angels. He goes to the cross by choice.

f.g: A Roman legion was about 6,000 soldiers — over 70,000 angels.

n: But then the scriptures about the Messiah’s suffering wouldn’t be fulfilled.
Jesus points out the absurdity: they come with weapons as if for a bandit, yet he taught openly in the temple every day.

f.g: As against a robber or rebel.

n: This too fulfills the prophets. Then all the disciples abandon him and run, just as he foretold.

f.w: all the disciples forsook him, and fled

n: Jesus is taken to Caiaphas, where the Jewish leaders have gathered at night.

f.g: John notes a preliminary hearing before Annas first.

n: Peter follows at a distance into the high priest’s courtyard and sits with the guards to see what happens.

f.g: To see how it would turn out.

n: The council seeks false testimony to justify a death sentence — a trial with the verdict decided beforehand.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member supreme Jewish council.

n: Many false witnesses come forward, but their stories don’t agree. The law required witnesses to agree. Finally two come forward.
They twist Jesus’s earlier words about destroying and rebuilding the temple. He had been speaking of his body.

f.w: I am able to destroy the temple of God

n: The high priest demands that Jesus respond to the charges.
Jesus stays silent, as Isaiah foretold. Then Caiaphas puts him under solemn oath: is he the Christ, the Son of God?

f.g: I put you under oath.

n: Jesus affirms it, then declares they will see him at God’s right hand and coming on the clouds — combining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7.

f.g: “Power” was a reverent substitute for God’s name.

n: The high priest tears his robes — a ritual sign of horror at blasphemy — and declares no more witnesses are needed.

f.g: rent = tore.

n: The council pronounces him deserving of death.
They spit in his face and beat him — the Judge of all being judged by men.

f.g: buffeted = struck with fists.

n: Blindfolded (as Mark notes), Jesus is mocked: “Prophesy — who hit you?”
Outside in the courtyard, a servant girl says Peter was with Jesus of Galilee.

f.g: without = outside.
A young servant girl.

n: Peter denies it in front of everyone, pretending not to understand.

f.w: I know not what thou sayest

n: At the gateway, another girl identifies him as a follower of Jesus of Nazareth.

f.g: The gateway or entrance passage.

n: Peter denies again, this time with an oath: “I don’t know the man.”
Bystanders say his Galilean accent gives him away.

f.g: bewrayeth = betrays, reveals.
His Galilean accent was distinct from Judean speech.

n: Peter calls down curses and swears he doesn’t know Jesus — and immediately the rooster crows.

f.g: To invoke a curse on himself if lying, and to take oaths.

n: Remembering Jesus’s words, Peter goes out and weeps bitterly. His sorrow leads to repentance; he will become a mighty witness.
